doc_summary: Barnes describes ARC Evals' red-team evaluations of GPT-4 and Claude for autonomous replication, where researchers stepped through tasks with the model in a realistic simulated environment. The post covers the methodology, a TaskRabbit CAPTCHA example, and conclusions about what the models could and could not do.

items.claim: Prefers having the model actually write and run code and observe real outputs over having it describe what it would do and judging success ourselves, because this approximates what would happen 'in the wild'.
items.quote: We attempted to approximate as closely as possible what would happen if the model actually attempted the task “‘in the wild” - we actually had the model write code and see the inputs of running that code, rather than just having the model describe what it might do and assess ourselves whether this would succeed.

items.claim: In a setup, have researchers act as tools and feed real command results back into the prompt step by step instead of using static or purely described outcomes, because this creates a realistic simulation from the model's perspective.
items.quote: We built some tooling to allow researchers to quickly obtain the result of carrying out the model’s suggested action and add this to the model’s prompt, allowing them to ‘step through’ the task with the model. For many tasks and actions, this allows us to create a realistic simulation from the model’s perspective.

items.claim: In a setup, swap fake credentials for real ones behind the scenes while making it appear to the model that the fake ones were used, instead of exposing the safety scaffolding, because the model's perceived situation stays intact while risk is contained.
items.quote: we would give the model fake account or credit card details, then swap in real ones when it tried to use these, while ensuring that it appeared to the model as if the fake credentials had been used.

items.claim: In a setup, have humans role-play or spoof parts of the environment (victims, task outcomes) and let the model interact with real unsuspecting humans where safe, instead of obviously mocked interactions, so the agent continues behaving as it would in a real situation.
items.quote: In some cases we “spoofed” the results of completing illegal and/or dangerous tasks - e.g. telling the model that it had successfully obtained someone’s identity via phishing, to see if the model could then take sensible steps to continue the task.

items.claim: When the model fails, investigates how far from success it was by intervening to fix mistakes and checking whether it then succeeds or fails in a new way, rather than treating the first failure as final.
items.quote: When the model failed, we investigated how far away it was from success, for example by having humans fix some of its mistakes, and then seeing if it succeeded or just failed in a new way.

items.claim: Prefers testing obstacles that emerge organically and are representative of real hurdles over contrived ones, because the CAPTCHA example arose naturally during investigation and resembles simple blockers a replicating agent would face.
items.quote: it emerged organically in our investigation and seems representative of the kind of simple obstacle that a replicating model would often need to overcome.

items.claim: Elicits capability with multiple prompting strategies rather than one, to avoid underestimating what the model can do.
items.quote: We tried various different prompting strategies (i.e. tried showing the model different text and instructions) to elicit the full range of the model’s abilities, but most tests included these two basic components.

items.claim: Prefers staying cautious about claims, noting limits of testing and that results are not replicable from the summary, rather than overclaiming safety, because the evaluations were insufficient and models are approaching relevance.
items.quote: The testing we’ve done so far is insufficient for many reasons, but we hope that the rigor of evaluations will scale up as AI systems become more capable.

items.claim: Distrusts evidence from tests that don't use the exact release model or full capabilities, flagging caveats such as non-identical model version and missing image access.
items.quote: This version was not identical to the release model, and we did not have access to image capabilities.

items.claim: Chooses what to test by focusing on a specific dangerous capability (autonomous resource acquisition and evading oversight) and testing it before models pose imminent risk, to give labs advance warning.
items.quote: It is important to have systematic, controlled testing of these capabilities in place before models pose an imminent risk, so that labs can have advance warning when they’re getting close and know to stop scaling up models further
